claims.text: Adding 3–5 at% tungsten together with a homogenization heat treatment will improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy.
The intervention will form fine tungsten-enriched intermetallic precipitates.
The tungsten-enriched precipitates will be thermally stable at elevated temperature.
The tungsten-enriched precipitates will inhibit grain-boundary sliding.
The tungsten-enriched precipitates will inhibit dislocation motion.
The proposed baseline is a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy containing no tungsten, with its other constituent elements present at 5–35 at% each.
A homogenization treatment can produce uniform tungsten dispersal and controlled precipitation of tungsten-rich phases.
Fine tungsten-enriched intermetallic precipitates will form along grain boundaries.
Tungsten can segregate to grain boundaries during heat treatment.
Tungsten-containing grain-boundary precipitates stabilize the alloy microstructure at high temperatures.
Microstructural stabilization and suppression of dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding enhance high-temperature strength and creep resistance.
Relative to the tungsten-free baseline, the tungsten-modified alloy will have higher yield strength at 700–900°C.
Relative to the tungsten-free baseline, the tungsten-modified alloy will have greater creep resistance at 700–900°C.
The expected elevated-temperature performance improvement is approximately 15–20%.
The predicted enhancement is limited to tungsten additions of 3–5 at% and operating temperatures of 700–900°C.

contradictions.description: The material definition requires constituent elements to be present at 5–35 at%, but the proposed tungsten range extends down to 3 at%. A modified alloy containing 3–<5 at% W would therefore fall outside the stated compositional definition.
